text.ask:
🔴 **Link matches beyond 100 are unreachable**

When a URL has over 100 matches, `find_links` caps every request at 100 without offering pagination. Clients cannot retrieve the remaining posts despite the reported `total`.

Learn more



`find_links` reads a bounded first page from `Store.links(to:limit:)` and reports the full count, but the tool has no cursor or offset argument. Increasing `limit` cannot advance past the first 100 results because `Args.int` clamps it. This is a permanent retrieval gap, not simply a compact default response.

**Example:** A URL shared by 140 posts returns 100 links and `total: 140`. Calling again with `limit: 140` returns the same 100; the other 40 cannot be requested.

**Recommended fix:** Add stable pagination to `Store.links(to:)` and expose an opaque cursor and `next_cursor` in `find_links`, with ordering that uniquely identifies each link row. Test traversal past 100 matches.

text.ask:
🟡 **Search results mix two database snapshots**

When sync commits between `store.search` and `store.posts`, `searchPosts` can return updated text that no longer matches the query. `total` and the cursor still describe the earlier snapshot, and a missing post disappears from the page.

Learn more



Search hits, count and cursor are computed in [search](https://github.com/laconicman/telegram-kb/blob/3950a115d3c916913e590bd1dc9e3768438e0a45/Sources/TelegramKBStore/Search.swift#L133-L183 "Sources/TelegramKBStore/Search.swift:133-183") inside one read snapshot. Hydration takes a second snapshot in [posts(ids:)](https://github.com/laconicman/telegram-kb/blob/3950a115d3c916913e590bd1dc9e3768438e0a45/Sources/TelegramKBStore/Search.swift#L223-L228 "Sources/TelegramKBStore/Search.swift:223-228"). A concurrent writer can change a matched post between them, so the result page combines old search metadata and new post content. `find_links` has the same split between `links(to:)` and hydration, yielding inconsistent snippets and dates after a sync.

**Example:** Search for `swift` returns an ID with `total: 1`; sync replaces that post's text with `kotlin` before hydration. The returned search record has a `kotlin` snippet under a `swift` query, with `index_moved_since_cursor: false` on this first page.

**Recommended fix:** Hydrate search and link hits inside the same short `dbPool.read` transaction that selects the hits and computes totals; expose a Store API returning hydrated page data or accept a read-scoped callback. Test a write between the previous two reads.

text.ask:
🟡 **Date filter drops final-second posts**

With a date-only `to`, `Args.date` ends the day at `23:59:59Z`. Posts timestamped after that instant but before midnight disappear from `search_posts`.

Learn more



The `to` parameter promises an inclusive calendar day. [SearchFilter.sql](https://github.com/laconicman/telegram-kb/blob/3950a115d3c916913e590bd1dc9e3768438e0a45/Sources/TelegramKBStore/SearchFilter.swift#L40-L45 "Sources/TelegramKBStore/SearchFilter.swift:40-45") uses `p.date <= ?`, so turning the upper bound into `23:59:59Z` excludes a timestamp with any fraction of the final second. Store dates are `Date` values and can retain fractional seconds, including dates supplied by other ingest sources.

**Example:** `to: "2026-09-24"` excludes a post dated `2026-09-24T23:59:59.500Z`; it belongs to the requested day.

**Recommended fix:** Represent date-only upper bounds as the next day's midnight with an exclusive comparison, preserving inclusive comparisons for explicit timestamps; alternatively represent the final instant at the database's actual date precision. Add a fractional-final-second case.

text.ask:
🟡 **Text-only clients see false pagination instructions**

On a final page, `render` compares the page size with `total` and asks clients to pass a nonexistent `next_cursor`. A zero-limit link count also says no posts exist despite a positive `total`.

Learn more



The search and link text renderers use `page.count < total` to decide whether another page exists. That comparison is true on every page when the total exceeds the page size, including the final page; the store instead determines continuation with `nextCursor`. For `find_links` with `limit: 0`, [render](https://github.com/laconicman/telegram-kb/blob/7bfc4aeabcda08cb0a86b5fe1f13cba6879de1b6/Sources/TelegramKBMCP/ToolHandler.swift#L213-L225 "Sources/TelegramKBMCP/ToolHandler.swift:213-225") returns `No posts link to that URL.` before even considering the positive total.

**Example:** Two posts match a URL and the client requests one per page. Page two returns its sole post with `next_cursor: nil`, but its text says `1 of 2 post(s) — pass next_cursor for the rest`. With `limit: 0`, it says no posts link to the URL despite `total: 2`.

**Recommended fix:** Pass `nextCursor` into both renderers and base continuation text on its presence. Handle count-only pages separately, stating the total rather than treating an empty page as an empty result set.

text.ask:
🔴 **Oversized limit terminates the server**

A floating-point `limit` above `Int.max` makes `Args.int` trap during conversion, before the page-size clamp runs. The MCP server exits instead of rejecting the argument.

Learn more



`limit` is a JSON number decoded as an MCP `Value`. A whole-valued double can exceed the range of Swift `Int`; checking whether it equals its rounded value does not make `Int(double)` safe. The conversion traps before the handler can return a result or `MCPError.invalidParams`.

**Example:** `search_posts` with `{"query":"swift","limit":1e20}` reaches the double branch; `1e20.rounded()` equals `1e20`, but converting it to `Int` terminates the process rather than clamping to 100.

**Recommended fix:** Check that the double is finite, nonnegative, integral, and representable before converting; alternatively clamp values above `max` in the double domain before conversion. Reject other numeric values with `MCPError.invalidParams`, and test a whole-valued number larger than `Int.max`.

text.ask:
🟡 **Shortener pagination fails after resolution changes**

When a queried shortener gains or changes resolution, `links(to:)` rejects its previous cursor as foreign. Its fingerprint changes with the resolved destination, so the client receives no page or `index_moved_since_cursor` warning.

Learn more



A link cursor carries a fingerprint of the match key and the index generation. A shortener's match key comes from its `urlResolution` row, which a writer can update between pages. The writer increments the generation in [upsert(resolutions:)](https://github.com/laconicman/telegram-kb/blob/7bfc4aeabcda08cb0a86b5fe1f13cba6879de1b6/Sources/TelegramKBStore/Store.swift#L243-L258 "Sources/TelegramKBStore/Store.swift:243-258"), but the changed match key causes `Cursor.resume` to throw before that generation can be compared. This turns ordinary corpus movement into an invalid-argument error instead of the advertised drift signal.

**Example:** A query for `https://clck.ru/x` returns page one while its resolution points to `https://a.example`. An import changes its destination to `https://b.example`; the same URL and cursor now yield `cursorDoesNotMatchQuery`, rather than a page marked as moved.

**Recommended fix:** Bind the cursor to the stable canonical query URL as well as the lookup mode, not its mutable resolved match key; retain the generation check to signal changed membership. Preserve equivalent-spelling cursor sharing where the effective key remains stable, and test a changed resolution of the queried URL between pages.

text.ask:
🟡 **Final pages violate their output schemas**

On a final page, `next_cursor` encodes as `null`, but both tool schemas declare it as a string. Schema-validating MCP clients reject otherwise successful search and link results.

Learn more



Both [SearchPostsOutput](https://github.com/laconicman/telegram-kb/blob/7bfc4aeabcda08cb0a86b5fe1f13cba6879de1b6/Sources/TelegramKBMCP/Records.swift#L56-L64 "Sources/TelegramKBMCP/Records.swift:56-64") and [FindLinksOutput](https://github.com/laconicman/telegram-kb/blob/7bfc4aeabcda08cb0a86b5fe1f13cba6879de1b6/Sources/TelegramKBMCP/Records.swift#L81-L89 "Sources/TelegramKBMCP/Records.swift:81-89") hold `next_cursor` as `String?`. Swift's synthesized `Encodable` omits optional keys when they are nil, rather than encoding JSON `null`. The declared output schema does not list `next_cursor` as required, so omitted keys are valid under the current schema. No bug here if the SDK encodes via the synthesized `Codable` conformance; verify the exact encoded `structuredContent` on a terminal page before changing the schema.

text.ask:
🟡 **Fractional-second search bounds are rejected**

When `from` or `to` contains fractional seconds, `date` rejects a valid ISO-8601 timestamp. The default `ISO8601FormatStyle` omits fractional seconds, so clients cannot filter at stored millisecond precision.

Learn more



`search_posts` accepts ISO-8601 date bounds, and the archive can retain fractional seconds. The default `Date.ISO8601FormatStyle()` used by [iso](https://github.com/laconicman/telegram-kb/blob/a595d78c8d9955b51d4e1b59239d14bb42763d84/Sources/TelegramKBMCP/ToolHandler.swift#L325 "Sources/TelegramKBMCP/ToolHandler.swift:325") parses timestamps without fractional seconds. The parser falls through to the date-only branch and rejects a valid fractional timestamp as `invalidParams`.

**Example:** A caller provides `to: "2023-11-14T23:59:59.500Z"` to include posts through half a second before midnight. The tool rejects the call instead of applying that bound.

**Recommended fix:** Try a format style with `includingFractionalSeconds: true` alongside the existing nonfractional style, and add an MCP test for a fractional bound.

text.ask:
🟡 **Final-day posts vanish from date-only searches**

For a post after 23:59:59.999, `date` ends a date-only `to` one millisecond before midnight. The inclusive filter omits that post even though its date is the requested day.

Learn more



A date-only `to` represents all posts on that calendar day. This upper bound is the final millisecond, but `Post.date` is a Foundation `Date` and the store does not round its values before persisting them in [write](https://github.com/laconicman/telegram-kb/blob/a595d78c8d9955b51d4e1b59239d14bb42763d84/Sources/TelegramKBStore/Store.swift#L107-L124 "Sources/TelegramKBStore/Store.swift:107-124"). An imported post can therefore carry a sub-millisecond timestamp after the chosen upper bound. The inclusive SQL comparison in [SearchFilter.sql](https://github.com/laconicman/telegram-kb/blob/a595d78c8d9955b51d4e1b59239d14bb42763d84/Sources/TelegramKBStore/SearchFilter.swift#L40-L45 "Sources/TelegramKBStore/SearchFilter.swift:40-45") excludes it.

**Example:** For `to: "2023-11-14"`, a post dated `2023-11-14T23:59:59.9995Z` falls outside the computed bound, although it belongs to November 14.

**Recommended fix:** Represent date-only upper bounds as an exclusive next-day bound (`p.date < nextMidnight`) rather than an inclusive approximation of the previous day. Preserve inclusive comparison for explicit timestamp bounds; add a boundary test with sub-millisecond dates.

text.ask:
🟡 **Search dates lose fractional timestamps**

For posts stamped between whole seconds, `PostSummary.date` drops the fraction. Reusing that displayed date as an inclusive `to` excludes the post itself.

Learn more



Search records expose the post's date, and the search tool accepts inclusive timestamp bounds with fractional seconds. The default ISO-8601 rendering omits the fraction from stored dates with millisecond precision. Other MCP date renderings use the same format at [the full post](https://github.com/laconicman/telegram-kb/blob/34433e31a235de95b598cc538eea06389c7ed600/Sources/TelegramKBMCP/Records.swift#L154 "Sources/TelegramKBMCP/Records.swift:154") and [link hits](https://github.com/laconicman/telegram-kb/blob/34433e31a235de95b598cc538eea06389c7ed600/Sources/TelegramKBMCP/ToolHandler.swift#L147 "Sources/TelegramKBMCP/ToolHandler.swift:147"), so the problem also affects those returned timestamps.

**Example:** A post dated `2023-11-14T23:59:59.500Z` is shown as `2023-11-14T23:59:59Z`. Searching with `to` set to that displayed date excludes it, although the caller chose the post's own date.

**Recommended fix:** Render all returned post dates using an ISO-8601 style that includes fractional seconds. Add a round-trip test using a stored post with a `.500` timestamp and reuse the returned date as an inclusive bound.
